UN General Assembly resolutions are not formal, binding sources of international law and are certainly not always customary law or equivalent to treaties. They can at most serve as evidence of state practice and opinio juris that may contribute to the formation of customary international law, depending on content, voting patterns, and subsequent conduct. Among the offered options, neither is correct, but the closest defensible position is that GA resolutions reflect customary law only when widely and consistently supported—not automatically.
